sections.html:
Hancock County is a rural corner of north-central Iowa where Garner holds the courthouse. The 2020 census counted 10,795 residents, well under the 15,402 recorded in 1940. The population skews older: the median age is 45.4, and 24.1 percent of people are 65 or over. Shrinking, aging places tend to produce a lot of dated houses that need work, and owners often discover that deferred repairs and a tax balance both stand between them and a conventional listing.

Forest City runs across the line into Winnebago County. The county that contains the parcel sends the bill, which puts a Forest City owner on the Winnebago side with a different treasurer entirely. Read the parcel location on your statement before you dial.

sections.h2: Who to call about property tax
sections.html:
Taxes are paid to the Hancock County Treasurer at 855 State Street, Garner, IA 50438 (the Courthouse). The counter is staffed 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., Monday through Friday, except holidays. The number is 641-923-3122. Anything about how your house was valued, or whether you qualify for an exemption, goes to the assessor's office, which is a separate office from the treasurer.

The county offers credits for elderly and disabled owners. Dollar limits get revised, so ask the office for today's figures before you plan around one.

• Fall installment: due September 1, delinquent October 1.
  • Spring installment: due March 1, delinquent April 1.
  • A single full-year payment is accepted in September.
  • Late owners are mailed a notice each November 1 and May 1.
  • Paying in person, a debit card adds $2.00 and a credit card adds 2.25 percent. Online, an eCheck runs $0.25, and cards carry those same charges.

A late installment collects 1.5 percent interest monthly, starting the day after it goes delinquent. Not getting a statement is no defense. State rules make the owner responsible for seeing that a bill arrives, so if nothing has shown up by late summer, phone the treasurer rather than wait.

If the assessed value looks wrong, put a written protest in front of the Board of Review between April 2 and April 30. Hancock's board has five members and sits on or about May 1, and you are entitled to a written ruling with its reasons.

Iowa Code 441.37 limits you to specific complaints. Pick the one that fits your situation, and say so plainly in the protest:

  • Similar property is valued lower, so yours is out of line.
  • The figure is higher than the law permits.
  • The classification is wrong, or the parcel should be exempt.
  • Someone made a mistake in the assessment.
  • Fraud was involved.

A bare statement that the number seems high rarely succeeds. Gather values for a few comparable houses close to yours and submit them with the protest.

Iowa is swapping the homestead credit for an exemption worth 10 percent of taxable value, no less than $5,500 and no more than $20,000, from assessment year 2026 onward. Owners 65 and older who want the 65-plus exemption must file a fresh application with the assessor, even when a credit was already attached to the property.

Rollback is the state's yearly adjustment that keeps taxable value growth to 3 percent across Iowa. The Iowa Taxpayers Research foundation illustrated it with a 2025 residential rollback of 44.5345 percent. Local levy rates are outside that limit, which is why a bill can climb in a year when rollback looks favorable.

The auction is online, held the third Monday of June beginning at 9:00 a.m. Bidders sign up at iowataxauction.com. Iowa Code chapter 446 requires the treasurer to put these parcels up for sale.

  • Around June 1 the parcel list is posted, and it is refreshed daily until the auction.
  • The June newspaper ad names the delinquent owners, and the publication fee lands on May 1 whether or not you pay later.
  • The county has to mail notice of the sale by May 1, addressed as the parcel is taxed.
  • The last day to pay and avoid being published shifts annually. Get the current cutoff from the treasurer.
  • To redeem a sold parcel you need guaranteed funds, and interest runs 2 percent each month.

Owners who are behind should act before the list goes up. Closing a sale first means the balance is settled from what you receive, rather than redeemed later at 2 percent a month.

Property tax trails the calendar by a year. At closing it is either split between the parties or the seller pays the treasurer separately. A closing from July 1 through December 31 leaves the September installment with the seller, and a closing from January 1 through June 30 leaves the March one. Back taxes are paid out of your proceeds, so the buyer takes the house free of them.

Expect the state's transfer tax too: 80 cents per $500 of value after the first $500 (Iowa Code 428A.1). A declaration of value goes to the county recorder with the deed, and the recorder hands it on to the assessor, who retains it for three years from the December 31 of the transfer year.

Before you list, collect your recent tax statements, any notice from the treasurer and the names of everyone on the title. The closing agent will ask for all of it, and having it ready spares you a scramble in the final week. If you are weighing a cash sale, bring the same folder to that conversation, because a buyer pricing a house as-is still needs to know what is owed against it.

Hancock County winters punish roofs, furnaces and plumbing. Forest City averages about 40.2 inches of snow a year. An inspector going through an older small-town house usually flags the roof, insulation, the heating system and a damp basement. Buyers with a mortgage often want these repaired or the price cut.

An as-is cash purchase skips that negotiation. Liens, back taxes and open permits do not disappear, though. They are cleared at the closing table whichever way the house sells, so find out what is attached to your parcel early, and the sale will move faster for you and for whoever buys. The treasurer can tell you what is owed, and the assessor can tell you how the house is classified and valued.

faqs.q: When are Hancock County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The fall installment is due September 1 and delinquent October 1. The spring installment is due March 1 and delinquent April 1. You may also pay the whole year in September.

faqs.q: Where is the Hancock County Treasurer?
faqs.a: The office is in the Courthouse at 855 State Street, Garner, Iowa 50438. It is open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., and the phone number is 641-923-3122.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to redeem a Hancock County tax sale parcel?
faqs.a: You pay the price the parcel sold for plus 2 percent interest for each month, using guaranteed funds. Ask the treasurer for an exact payoff figure.

faqs.q: Is Forest City in Hancock County?
faqs.a: Partly. The city spans Hancock and Winnebago counties, and the county containing your parcel decides which treasurer sends the bill.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to protest my Hancock County assessment?
faqs.a: The written protest goes to the Board of Review between April 2 and April 30. The board meets on or about May 1 and must answer in writing.
